questions.q: The old docs script "finished without errors" while publishing a broken link and an internal runbook. What was missing?
questions.explain: To a script that copies files, docs are only text, so nothing can be wrong. Once each page is a document with an id, metadata and links that can be resolved, a check can fail the build, the same way a failing test does.
options: A structure for the pages and an automatic check of that structure, as code has a type checker and tests
A bigger server for the website

questions.q: Why should a document's id stay the same when its title changes?
questions.explain: The title is what readers see and may be reworded freely. The id is the page's address. When you must change it, keep a redirect from the old id.
options: Because ids must be unique and titles need not be
Links, navigation entries, URLs and bookmarks all point at the id; changing it breaks every one of them
Because the title is not stored

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: documentIdFromPath turns separators into dots and removes only the final extension, so the folder v1.2 becomes two segments. Ids are dot-separated segments of letters, digits, _ and -, so a hyphen is fine and a slash is not.

questions.q: Given the previous answer, which two files would end up with the same id?
questions.explain: Both become guides.v1.2.routing. start.md and start.mdx would also collide, as the extension is dropped. The registry refuses the second one with DuplicateDocumentError, which is exactly how such a collision is found.
options: No two paths can ever give the same id

questions.q: Documents from createDocument are deep-frozen. What does that protect against?
questions.explain: A docs build passes the same page objects to validators, generators and indexes. If one step could change a page, the others would see different data depending on the order they run in. Frozen documents are values, and a step that wants a change builds a new document.
options: Pages being deleted from the registry
Code in one part of the build changing a page (its tags, its content) that other parts are also reading

questions.q: What does parseFrontmatter return as metadata here?
questions.explain: tags is always a list. version is always a string. Other values become numbers only when nothing is lost: 3 is safe, but 2.10 would become 2.1 and 007 would become 7, so those stay strings.

questions.q: A Markdown file from a contributor has __proto__: admin in its frontmatter. What does parseFrontmatter do with it?
questions.explain: Keys that could alter an object's prototype (__proto__, constructor, prototype) are refused. Frontmatter is input, and input must never be able to change how your objects behave. This is prototype pollution, defended by the parser.
options: Sets the prototype of the metadata object
Leaves the key out of the result, so no object's prototype can be changed
Stores it as a normal property named __proto__

questions.q: A file starts with --- and a title, but the closing --- is missing. What does parseFrontmatter return?
questions.explain: Only a well-formed block is read. A broken one is not guessed at. The page then has no title from frontmatter, and the loader falls back to the first heading or the file name, or validation reports it.
options: Empty metadata and the whole text unchanged as content; the missing title shows up later in validation
The title, and the rest as content

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The serializer quotes a value only when its own parser would read it back differently. "5000" would come back as a number, so it is quoted. yes is not a boolean for this parser, so it is written plainly.
questions.code:
import { serializeFrontmatter } from "@zudojs/docs";
console.log(serializeFrontmatter({ title: "Refunds", price: "5000", public: "yes" }, "# Refunds\n"));
options:
---
title: Refunds
price: "5000"
public: yes
---

# Refunds

---
title: Refunds
price: 5000
public: yes
---

# Refunds

---
title: Refunds
price: 5000
public: true
---

# Refunds

questions.q: Frontmatter said category: payments. What does this print?
questions.explain: createDocument checks the id, title and content, not the category. The document is built, and validateDocument reports the unknown category. That is why the loader can cast frontmatter strings, as long as validation runs afterwards.

questions.q: Why does the lesson generate the error reference from the @zudojs/errors classes instead of writing it in Markdown?
questions.explain: A hand-written copy of facts that live in code goes stale the first time someone changes the code and forgets the docs. Generating the page removes the copy. The same works for config keys, routes, events and CLI commands.
options: The status codes and error codes live in the code; a page built from them changes when they change, so it cannot drift
Because the registry only accepts structured documents

questions.q: Structured content comes from a JSON file that partners can edit. What does this print?
questions.explain: Every value is escaped for its position: the | is escaped so the cell stays one cell, and a link whose scheme is not on the allow-list is written as plain text. Untrusted structured content cannot break the table or become a live javascript: link.
options:
| Plan | Price |
| --- | --- |
| Basic \| Monthly | ₦5,000 |

Pay now

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The registry refuses a second page with the same id and keeps the first one. It never silently replaces a page, which is how two files that map to the same URL are found.

questions.q: One page says visibility: "server" in lower case. What does this print?
questions.explain: The filter fails closed: only an unset visibility or exactly "CLIENT" is public. The typo "server" is treated as internal. A mistake hides a page; it never publishes one.

questions.q: Why is "fail closed" the right default for visibility?
questions.explain: Compare the costs of the two mistakes. Someone notices a missing page and fixes it. A leaked runbook may already be in search engines and caches. When one direction of error is much worse, the default should avoid it.
options: A wrongly hidden public page is a small, visible problem; a wrongly published internal page cannot be taken back once it is indexed
Because it makes the filter faster
Because "CLIENT" is the only valid value

questions.q: How are these relative links resolved?
questions.explain: An id works like a file path: guides.auth.login is the file login in the folder guides/auth. ./ stays in that folder, ../ goes up one, slashes become dots, and the #fragment is removed.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: ./login resolves to guides.login, which does not exist, but a broken link is only a warning, so valid stays true. The external link is skipped entirely. A CI check that looks at valid alone would let this through.

questions.q: Given that broken links are warnings, what does the lesson's checkDocs do?
questions.explain: The package reports; your project decides the policy. For a public docs site, a dead link is a real defect, so the check fails on every issue. You can also fail only on chosen codes, such as BROKEN_LINK and NAVIGATION_ORPHAN_DOCUMENT.
options: Counts every issue, warnings included, and fails when there is any
Retries the check until the warnings go away

questions.q: A public page links to ../../internal/runbook, which exists. Why does the lesson's check still report it as a broken link?
questions.explain: Validating the "CLIENT" pages as their own set turns "links to an internal page" into "links to a missing page". That is exactly what a reader of the public site would see: a 404.
options: Because the runbook has no title
Public pages are validated against the public ids only; for the public site the runbook does not exist, and the link would also reveal it
Because relative links are not allowed
Because the runbook is in a different folder

questions.q: What is validateLinks's UNSAFE_LINK check good for, and what is it not?
questions.explain: It reads Markdown link syntax, not every way HTML can end up in a page, and it only reports. Pages written by people outside your team need a real HTML sanitizer at render time; the lint helps your own authors catch mistakes early.
options: It makes any rendered page safe from script injection
It is a useful lint that flags Markdown links with schemes like javascript:; it does not replace sanitizing the rendered HTML
It checks that external websites are online
It removes unsafe links from the document

questions.q: Which of these links does validateLinks not check against the registry?
questions.explain: Links with a safe scheme such as https: point outside your docs and cannot be checked without the network; links inside code blocks are examples, not links. Relative and bare targets are resolved and looked up.
options: [the site](https://example.com) and a link inside a fenced code block

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Breadcrumbs walk from the top to the page. The flattened list contains every page in reading order, including the "Reference" section page. getAdjacent only looks at the same level, and "Tasks" is the last page inside Guides, so it has no next page there.

questions.q: Why is the navigation tree kept separate from the documents instead of each page saying where it belongs?
questions.explain: One tree is easy to review and to validate. If order and grouping were spread over dozens of files, a reorder would touch all of them, and nothing would notice two pages claiming the same position.
options: So the sidebar can be reordered and regrouped in one place, and checked as a whole (unknown pages, cycles, orphans)
Because the navigation is only used on mobile
Because pages without a section cannot be registered

questions.q: validateAll(pages, navigation) reports NAVIGATION_ORPHAN_DOCUMENT. What happened?
questions.explain: Orphans are usually new pages someone forgot to add to the sidebar, as with the "Logging out" page in the lesson. Validate internal pages without a navigation, because they are not meant to be in the public sidebar.
options: A page exists but no navigation item points to it, so readers can only reach it by a direct link
A navigation item has no title
A page has no parent folder

questions.q: What does validateExample tell you about a code example?
questions.explain: It checks the shape of the example object. Running examples is a separate job, done by a test suite, which is how every example in this academy is kept correct.
options: That the code runs without errors
That it has an id, a language and some code; whether it works is for your tests to check
That its output matches the documentation

questions.q: An example's code contains ```. How does renderExampleMarkdown keep it from closing its own code block?
questions.explain: Markdown closes a fence only with a fence at least as long as the opening one. Choosing a longer fence keeps the example intact without changing a single character of the code.
options: It escapes every backtick with a backslash
It uses a fence longer than any run of backticks inside the code, such as four backticks

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: generateIndex includes only client-visible pages unless you ask for more. Even when a build passes it every page, the default index cannot leak an internal one.

questions.q: What does stripMarkdown produce for a search entry?
questions.explain: Headings, emphasis, code marks and link syntax are removed, and the visible text stays, line breaks included. That plain text is what a search index should match against.
questions.code:
import { stripMarkdown } from "@zudojs/docs";
console.log(JSON.stringify(stripMarkdown("## Refunds\n\nSend **POST** `/refunds` — see [the guide](./refunds).")));

questions.q: The build keeps the runbook out of the public output in three ways. Which one is not among them?
questions.explain: Several independent guards mean one mistake (a missing filter, a wrong option) is not enough to leak a page. Encryption plays no part; internal pages are protected by never being published.
options: The build only takes "CLIENT" pages from the registry
The check refuses public links to internal pages
The runbook file is encrypted on disk

questions.q: The docs test "document every status the API sends" compares the generated table with ["400", "401", "403", "404", "409"]. When does it fail?
questions.explain: The page is generated from a list of classes, and that list is still written by a person. The test pins the list to what the API really sends, so adding a TooManyRequestsError without documenting it fails the build.
options: Every time the docs are built
When the API starts using another error, or stops using one, and the list of error classes in the reference is not updated
Never, because the page is generated

questions.q: Why should links to other websites be checked in a separate, scheduled job rather than in the docs check on every commit?
questions.explain: The per-commit check must be deterministic: same input, same result. External links depend on the outside world, so check them on a schedule, with retries, and open an issue when one stays broken.
options: Because external links are always correct
Checking them needs the network, which is slow and flaky; a commit should not fail because someone else's site was down for a minute
Because the package forbids external links

questions.q: Write failsBuild(result): return true when the result has any error, or any warning whose code is in FAIL_ON. Other warnings are allowed.
questions.explain: The second result is valid: true, but its broken link is on your list, so the build fails. Looking at valid alone would pass it. A policy based on codes lets you choose which warnings matter to your site.

questions.q: Write idFromPath(path): turn / and \ into dots and remove the .md or .mdx extension of the last segment only.
questions.explain: Removing the extension first, anchored with $, touches only the end of the path, so the folder v1.2 keeps its dot. Handling both separators makes the build give the same ids on Windows and on Linux.

questions.q: Write resolveLink(baseId, link) like the package's resolver: the base id's folder is everything but its last segment; ./ stays there, each ../ goes up one level; slashes in the rest become dots; a #fragment is removed.
questions.explain: Treating ids as paths is what lets authors write the same relative links they would use between files. Each .. removes one folder, each name adds one, and the fragment only matters to the browser, not to which page is meant.

questions.q: Frontmatter tags arrive in three shapes: a list, a single string, or nothing. Write toTags(value) that always returns an array of trimmed, non-empty strings, so a single tag never becomes a list of letters.
questions.explain: Spreading a string gives its characters, which is the bug the starter shows: "payments" would become eight one-letter tags. @zudojs/docs fixed exactly this in its parser and builder; any code that reads frontmatter itself must do the same.

questions.q: Write flatten(items): return every documentId in the navigation tree in reading order (a section's own page before its children), each id only once.
questions.explain: A depth-first walk that visits the item before its children gives reading order. A Set keeps each page once, at its first position; add on an existing value does not move it. flattenNavigation also guards against cycles and very deep trees.

questions.q: Write breadcrumbs(id, items): return the titles from the top of the tree down to the item with that documentId, or an empty array when it is not in the tree.
questions.explain: The recursion returns the path found below an item, and each level puts its own title in front. An empty result means "not under here", so the search moves on to the next item. The package's getBreadcrumbs also returns the documentId of each level, so section pages stay linkable.
questions.expected:
Guides › Authentication › Sessions and tokens
Reference › Error codes
[]

questions.q: Write fenceFor(code): return a run of backticks one longer than the longest run of backticks in code, and at least three.
questions.explain: A code block ends at the first fence at least as long as the opening one. If the opening fence is longer than anything inside, the content can never close it. Math.max(0, …) covers code with no backticks at all.

questions.q: Write search(entries, query): 3 points per query word found in the title, 1 point per word found in the content (both lower-cased), keep pages with points, and sort by score (highest first), then by id. Print the ids.
questions.explain: "session" is in the sessions page's title and text (4 points) and only in the login page's text (1 point). For "assign tasks", the tasks page gets 1 for "assign" in its text and 3 + 1 for "tasks". The id tie-breaker keeps equal scores in a stable order.
